entries.question: Were the men with Paul knocked to the ground?
entries.summary: Acts gives three accounts of Paul's Damascus road encounter and they don't line up. In Acts 26:14 Paul tells Agrippa everyone in the party fell to the ground. In Acts 9:7 the narrator reports that Paul's companions stood speechless. Same author, same event, two physically incompatible postures.
entries.commentary: This is a triple-telling problem. Luke narrates the conversion in Acts 9, then has Paul retell it before the Jerusalem mob in Acts 22, then again before Agrippa in Acts 26. The details shift each time. In 9:7 the men stand and hear the voice but see nothing. In 22:9 they see the light but don't hear the voice. In 26:14 they're all knocked down. Apologists like Gleason Archer and Norman Geisler typically run a two-step harmonization here. Step one: maybe everyone fell at first and then got up, so 9:7 is just describing a later moment. Step two: the Greek verb in 9:7 (heistēkeisan, pluperfect of histēmi with stative force) just means "remained" rather than literally "stood," so it doesn't necessarily contradict 26:14. The first move is pure imagination — the text doesn't describe a sequence, it describes a state. The second move strains the lexicon; the perfect/pluperfect of histēmi regularly carries the standing-on-feet meaning (BDAG s.v. ἵστημι), and the contrast with everyone-fell in 26:14 is exactly what makes the tension obvious. Critical scholars including Ernst Haenchen and Hans Conzelmann read the three accounts as Luke's literary reworking, not stenographic transcripts. Luke is a theological storyteller adapting the conversion narrative to fit each rhetorical setting — apology before a Jewish crowd, apology before a Roman king — and the surface details get moved around in the process. The contradiction is real because Luke wasn't writing a court deposition.

entries.question: Was Abraham justified by faith or works?
entries.summary: Paul and James pick the same proof text — Genesis 15:6 — and push it in opposite directions. Romans 4:2 explicitly says Abraham was not justified by works. James 2:21 explicitly says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac. Two New Testament writers using one Old Testament figure to make incompatible soteriological claims.
entries.commentary: This is one of the oldest internal-NT debates in church history and the one that nearly kept James out of the canon. Luther famously called James a "right strawy epistle" precisely because he could not square James 2:21-24 with Romans 3-4. The standard apologetic move, found in everyone from Calvin to Douglas Moo, says Paul and James are using "justify" and "works" in different senses. Paul means initial declaration of righteousness apart from works of Torah; James means demonstration of genuine faith through subsequent action. On this reading, the two are complementary — Paul attacks legalism, James attacks dead orthodoxy. The problem is that both authors quote Genesis 15:6 (Rom 4:3; Jas 2:23) and reach grammatically opposite verdicts on the same Abrahamic episode. Paul's whole argument in Romans 4:2-5 hinges on Abraham *not* being justified by works, full stop, because that's what protects boasting from creeping back in. James 2:24 then states the inverse with equal directness: "a person is justified by works and not by faith alone." Critical scholars including James Dunn, Luke Timothy Johnson, and Dale Allison have argued that James is not just complementing Paul — he is correcting a Paulinist reading, possibly a misreading, that had begun circulating. The two authors come from different streams of early Christianity with different relationships to Jewish-Christian practice, and the redactional history of the canon papered over a genuine theological dispute. The harmonization works only if you assume a coherence the texts themselves resist.

entries.question: Who was to blame for original sin?
entries.summary: 1 Timothy 2:14 pins the fall on Eve and explicitly says Adam was not deceived. Romans 5:12 puts the entire entry of sin and death into the world on "one man" — Adam. Two Pauline-tradition letters single out two different culprits for the same event, and the 1 Timothy version functions as the basis for restricting women in the assembly.
entries.commentary: These two passages have shaped two thousand years of Christian gender theology and they don't agree. Romans 5:12-21 builds a strict Adam-Christ typology where Adam is *the* gateway for sin and death and Christ is the gateway for righteousness — Eve doesn't appear in the argument at all. 1 Timothy 2:13-14 inverts this completely and uses the deception of Eve, not Adam, as the rationale for forbidding women to teach. Traditional harmonizers like Wayne Grudem and Andreas Köstenberger argue that the two texts address different facets of the same event: Adam bears federal-headship responsibility (Romans), Eve bears chronological priority of deception (1 Timothy). The problem is that 1 Timothy 2:14 doesn't just note that Eve was deceived — it explicitly contrasts her with Adam, who "was not deceived," effectively letting him off the deception hook. Critical scholarship has long noted that 1 Timothy is widely regarded as deutero-Pauline; the standard view from Bart Ehrman, Margaret MacDonald, and Raymond Collins is that the Pastorals were written by a later author in Paul's name, in a more rigid ecclesial setting, who is reworking Genesis 3 to bolster a patriarchal church order Paul himself never articulated. The contradiction isn't theological hairsplitting between two complementary truths — it's two different authors, separated by decades, with different agendas, both authorized in scripture. Genesis 3 itself, by the way, doesn't excuse either party.

entries.question: Who was God's firstborn son?
entries.summary: The Bible designates three different figures as God's firstborn. Exodus 4:22 calls Israel God's firstborn son. Jeremiah 31:9 says it is Ephraim. Romans 8:29 and Colossians 1:15 transfer the title to Jesus. The label is supposed to mark a unique, singular status, but it gets reassigned across the canon.
entries.commentary: "Firstborn" (Hebrew *bekor*, Greek *prototokos*) is not a casual title in the Hebrew Bible — it carries legal and theological weight including priority of inheritance and covenantal favor. Exodus 4:22 deploys it nationally; Yahweh's claim on Israel is what justifies the death of Egypt's firstborn. Jeremiah 31:9, written centuries later in a Northern-restoration context, transfers the title to Ephraim — the dominant tribe of the northern kingdom — even though Ephraim was literally the *younger* son of Joseph (Gen 48:14). The New Testament then reassigns the title again to Jesus in Pauline and deutero-Pauline contexts. Apologetic harmonization typically appeals to a non-literal sense: "firstborn" connotes preeminence rather than chronological priority, so multiple figures can hold the title in different aspects (so Murray Harris, F. F. Bruce). That works for some cases — *prototokos* in Col 1:15 plainly invokes status, not chronology — but it doesn't resolve the Israel-versus-Ephraim tension, where both are corporate entities with covenantal claims. Critical scholarship from Jon Levenson and Brevard Childs treats the multiple firstborn designations as evidence of a developing theology that repeatedly recoded chosen-ness for new political and theological situations. The Ephraim claim reflects Northern self-understanding; the Israel claim reflects Exodus-tradition national identity; the Jesus claim represents the early Christian movement reassigning Israel's distinctives to its messianic figure. The harmonization works only if you read "firstborn" as elastic enough to mean almost nothing.

entries.question: Is it OK to curse people?
entries.summary: Romans 12:14 commands believers to bless and not curse, with no exception clause. Paul himself then breaks that rule. In 1 Corinthians 16:22 he pronounces anathema on anyone who does not love the Lord, and in Galatians 1:8-9 he pronounces it twice on anyone preaching a different gospel — even an angel.
entries.commentary: This isn't two authors disagreeing — this is Paul disagreeing with Paul. Romans 12:14 echoes Jesus' Sermon on the Mount teaching: "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." Paul's language uses *katarasthe* (curse) absolutely, no qualifier. Then in Galatians 1:8-9 he uses *anathema estō* twice — let him be accursed — against rival missionaries. 1 Corinthians 16:22 does the same to anyone who doesn't love Christ. Harmonizers like Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner draw a distinction between personal animosity (forbidden in Rom 12:14) and ecclesial sanction or eschatological judgment (permitted in Gal 1:8 and 1 Cor 16:22). The idea is that Paul is invoking divine judgment, not personal vindictiveness. That distinction is real in later Christian theology, but it isn't textually marked in Romans 12:14 — the verse offers no exception for theological opponents. Critical scholarship from J. Louis Martyn and Hans Dieter Betz has long noted that Galatians is a polemical white-knuckle letter where Paul's emotional register is raw and the rhetoric is closer to first-century juridical curse formulas than to measured pastoral instruction. Paul is a polemicist who, like any polemicist, applies his own principles selectively when his theology is under attack. The contradiction is psychological as much as exegetical: Paul preaches bless-not-curse, then curses anyone who threatens his gospel. The harmonization rescues consistency only by importing categories Paul didn't supply.

entries.question: Should we try to please others?
entries.summary: Romans 15:2 tells believers each one of us should please his neighbor for his good. 1 Corinthians 10:33 has Paul claiming he himself pleases all people in all things. Galatians 1:10 then has Paul deny this categorically — if he still pleased men, he would not be a servant of Christ. The same author, the same verb (areskō), opposite directives.
entries.commentary: The contradiction here is internal to Paul and runs across the verb *areskō* in three of his letters. In Galatians 1:10 Paul is defending his apostolic credentials against opponents who apparently accuse him of softening his message to win human approval — and he denies it with the famous "if I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ." Meanwhile in Romans 15:2 and 1 Corinthians 10:33 he is exhorting the same kind of accommodating behavior he repudiates in Galatians. The standard harmonization, articulated by F. F. Bruce and Richard Longenecker, distinguishes motive: please others *for their good* (Rom 15) is altruistic, please others *for your own approval* (Gal 1:10) is self-serving. That distinction is plausible at the level of intent, but it papers over the textual surface — Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:33 says he pleases all people in all things, full stop, and Galatians 1:10 explicitly contrasts pleasing men with serving Christ as if the two were structurally opposed. Hans Dieter Betz and J. Louis Martyn read Galatians 1 as polemical self-defense where Paul is overcorrecting against accusations. The Romans/Corinthians language reflects Paul's pastoral mode in less embattled correspondence. The contradiction isn't fatal to Paul's overall theology, but it does show that his rhetoric on accommodation shifts dramatically depending on whether he is under attack. A consistent ethic of "please your neighbor for their good" cannot survive contact with Galatians 1:10's absolute rejection of people-pleasing without importing a motive distinction the text doesn't supply.

entries.question: Is God the author of confusion?
entries.summary: 1 Corinthians 14:33 states flatly that God is not the author of confusion. But Genesis 11:7-9 has Yahweh deliberately confounding human language at Babel so the people will not understand one another, and 1 Corinthians 1:27 has God choosing foolish things specifically to confound the wise. The same epistle that denies confusion also describes God deploying it.
entries.commentary: The Hebrew verb in Genesis 11:7 is *balal*, "to confuse, mix up" — a divinely engineered cognitive disruption to scatter humanity. The Greek verb in 1 Corinthians 1:27 is *kataischynō*, often translated "shame" but functionally meaning to confound or disgrace the wise — and Paul makes God the subject. Then in 1 Corinthians 14:33 Paul writes *ou gar estin akatastasias ho theos*, "God is not of disorder." The English word "confusion" papers over what are actually distinct Greek and Hebrew concepts. Apologists like Norman Geisler argue the contradiction dissolves once you recognize three different semantic ranges: linguistic scattering in Genesis, rhetorical shaming in 1 Cor 1, and liturgical disorder in 1 Cor 14. That distinction is genuine, and a charitable reading can accommodate it. But the SAB-style question is whether the popular English-Bible reader, encountering the same word "confound/confuse" across these passages in the KJV, ends up with a coherent picture of God's relationship to confusion — and on that surface level, no. Critical scholarship treats Babel as one of the J-source etiologies explaining linguistic diversity through divine intervention (so Speiser, Westermann), and treats 1 Corinthians 1:27 as Paul reworking Isaiah-style reversal motifs. The tension is mostly a translation artifact, but it's also a substantive theological tension: a God who scatters languages and shames the wise is engaged in cognitive disruption, even if the Greek for liturgical disorder in 14:33 is technically a different word. Worth a coherency note that the "confusion" link is partly lexical.

entries.question: What is the foundation of the church?
entries.summary: 1 Corinthians 3:11 declares Jesus Christ to be the foundation, and adds that no one can lay any other foundation. Ephesians 2:20 says the household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the chief cornerstone — not the foundation itself. The two passages disagree about both what the foundation is and what Christ's relationship to it is.
entries.commentary: Both texts come from the Pauline corpus but they use the construction-metaphor language differently. 1 Corinthians 3:10-11 is Paul defending his own foundational ministry against rival teachers in Corinth: I laid the foundation as a wise master builder, and that foundation is Jesus Christ. The grammar is exclusive — *themelion gar allon oudeis dynatai theinai* — no other foundation can be laid. Ephesians 2:19-20 expands the metaphor in a different direction: the household is built *epi tō themeliō tōn apostolōn kai prophētōn*, on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the *akrogōniaiou* (cornerstone). Apologetic harmonizers like Harold Hoehner and Peter O'Brien argue the genitive in Ephesians is appositional or epexegetical (the foundation *which is* the apostles and prophets — but understood as their proclamation of Christ), so Christ remains the substantive foundation in both passages. That's a grammatically possible reading, but it's not the more natural one; the more natural reading is the genitive of source or possession, making the apostles and prophets the foundation themselves. Critical scholarship widely treats Ephesians as deutero-Pauline (Ernest Best, Margaret MacDonald, Andrew Lincoln, with Markus Barth and Hoehner dissenting in favor of Pauline authorship), written by a later author developing Pauline themes into a more institutional ecclesiology where the apostles function as historical pillars. That shift in ecclesiology — from charismatic Pauline congregations where Christ alone is foundational to institutionalized Pauline-tradition churches where the apostles and prophets are constitutive — produces exactly the tension between these two verses. Ephesians is doing church-as-institution; 1 Corinthians 3 is doing Christ-as-sole-foundation.

entries.question: Is all Scripture inspired by God?
entries.summary: 2 Timothy 3:16 claims all scripture is God-breathed. But Paul himself in 1 Corinthians 7:12 distinguishes his teaching from the Lord's ("to the rest speak I, not the Lord") and in 7:25 admits he has no commandment from the Lord on virgins, only his own judgment. 2 Maccabees 15:39 has its author apologizing for any imperfections in his writing. Three counter-examples where authors disclaim divine inspiration in their own texts.
entries.commentary: This contradiction has serious implications for any robust doctrine of biblical inerrancy. 2 Timothy 3:16 — *pasa graphē theopneustos* — is the locus classicus for the doctrine of plenary verbal inspiration. But when you cross-reference Paul's own letters, Paul repeatedly distinguishes what he is saying on his own authority from what he is saying on the Lord's authority. 1 Corinthians 7:10-12 explicitly separates the two: "To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord)... To the rest I say (I, not the Lord)." 1 Corinthians 7:25 escalates: "Concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." The author of 2 Maccabees ends his work asking forgiveness if his composition is imperfect — a self-disclaimer hard to reconcile with theopneustic inspiration. Apologetic responses, from B. B. Warfield onward, argue that Paul's distinction between his own judgment and the Lord's reflects which traditions are dominical sayings — sayings from Jesus' earthly ministry — versus Paul's own apostolic ruling, but the latter is still inspired in the canonical sense. That works at a confessional level but it ignores Paul's own surface meaning: he is distinguishing levels of authority precisely because he doesn't think his ruling carries the same weight as a dominical command. Critical scholars including Bart Ehrman and James D. G. Dunn note that 2 Timothy is likely deutero-Pauline, written after Paul's death, and the inspiration claim in 3:16 was made about Jewish scripture (the LXX), not about a New Testament canon that didn't yet exist. The author of 2 Timothy is not making a claim about Paul's own letters, and Paul himself wouldn't have endorsed flat plenary verbal inspiration as later doctrine framed it. The 2 Maccabees citation is also relevant for Catholic and Orthodox canons that include it as scripture.

entries.question: Is it OK to marry unbelievers?
entries.summary: 1 Corinthians 7:12-14 has Paul instruct believers not to leave unbelieving spouses, and even says the unbelieving partner is sanctified by the believer. 2 Corinthians 6:14-17 forbids being unequally yoked with unbelievers and demands separation. Two letters from the same author to the same congregation produce diametrically opposed verdicts on cross-faith intimacy.
entries.commentary: The textual problem here intersects with one of the most contested questions in Pauline scholarship: is 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 even from Paul? In 1 Corinthians 7:12-14 Paul is unambiguous — a believing spouse should not leave the unbelieving partner; in fact, the unbeliever is *hēgiastai* (sanctified) by the believer, and the children are *hagia* (holy). This is a remarkably permissive theology of mixed marriage. Then in 2 Corinthians 6:14-17 the language flips entirely: "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers... come out from among them and be separate." Apologetic harmonization, articulated by writers like Murray Harris, distinguishes scenarios: 1 Corinthians 7 addresses existing marriages that pre-date conversion, while 2 Corinthians 6 prohibits forming new intimate alliances with unbelievers. That scenario distinction is plausible at a pastoral level, but the 2 Corinthians passage extends well beyond marriage to all close partnerships with unbelievers, including the language of "touch not the unclean thing," which is in direct conceptual tension with 1 Corinthians 7:14 where unbelievers are *sanctified* through the marriage relationship. Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz, Victor Furnish, and Margaret Thrall has long argued that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 is a non-Pauline interpolation — its vocabulary is anomalously Qumran-like, its theology of separation contradicts Paul's surrounding argument in 2 Corinthians, and removing it produces a smoother narrative flow. If that text-critical judgment is correct, the contradiction dissolves at the level of authorship but remains a contradiction within the canonical text. Either way, what canonical readers receive is two incompatible directives.

entries.question: Should you speak in tongues?
entries.summary: 1 Corinthians 14:5 has Paul saying he wishes all the Corinthians spoke in tongues and that anyone who speaks in tongues edifies himself. A few verses later in 14:8-9 he ridicules unintelligible speech as a trumpet giving an uncertain sound — words spoken into the air. The same chapter both endorses and discourages the practice.
entries.commentary: This is actually a softer contradiction than the SAB framing suggests, and is worth a coherency note. Paul's whole argument in 1 Corinthians 14 is not for-or-against tongues but a structured argument for *prophecy over tongues in the public assembly* because intelligibility builds the church. He affirms tongues as private edification (14:2, 14:5, 14:18 — "I thank God I speak in tongues more than all of you"), then argues that in the assembly, prophecy is greater because it builds others up. The 14:8-9 trumpet image isn't a blanket rejection of tongues — it's a rejection of *uninterpreted* tongues in corporate worship. Apologetic and most critical readings agree on this point: Gordon Fee, Anthony Thiselton, and Joseph Fitzmyer all treat the chapter as internally coherent once you respect Paul's public-versus-private distinction. Where the contradiction genuinely lives is in 14:39's command "do not forbid speaking in tongues" versus the broader Pauline silence on tongues outside Corinthians and the apparent decline of the practice in the post-apostolic period. The SAB-style reading flattens Paul's intentional tension into a flat contradiction. The chapter is better read as a regulated endorsement than as a self-contradiction, which means this entry overstates the conflict. There is real tension between Paul's enthusiasm for tongues in 14:5/14:18 and his strong push for intelligible speech, but framing the chapter as yes-vs-no misreads Paul's pastoral strategy.

entries.question: Did Paul see Jesus?
entries.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:1 and 15:8 unambiguously claims to have seen Jesus. Acts 9:8 says that when Paul opened his eyes on the Damascus road he saw no man and had to be led by the hand into Damascus. Paul's first-person testimony and Luke's narrative description of the same event contradict each other on what Paul actually saw.
entries.commentary: Paul stakes his apostolic legitimacy on having seen the risen Jesus. In 1 Corinthians 9:1 the rhetorical question "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" assumes the answer yes. In 1 Corinthians 15:8 he places himself last in a list of resurrection appearance recipients — *eschaton de pantōn ōphthē kamoi*. Acts 9:8, however, describes the moment Paul rises from the ground and opens his eyes: he saw no one, and his companions had to lead him by the hand into Damascus. Apologists like Gleason Archer and Norman Geisler reconcile by noting that Acts 9:3-7 describes the actual encounter with the light and the voice — and Paul did see something there — while 9:8 describes the *post-encounter* moment of physical blindness. That harmonization is reasonable for Acts itself, but it doesn't fully address the underlying tension. Critical scholarship from John Knox, Hans Conzelmann, and Alan Segal notes that Acts 9 doesn't actually describe Paul *seeing* Jesus — it describes a light, a voice, and a subsequent blindness. Paul's own language in 1 Cor 15:8 (*ōphthē*) is the same passive form used of the other resurrection appearances and connotes a visionary or revelatory seeing rather than ordinary visual perception. Luke and Paul are operating with different conceptions of what the Damascus event was: Paul calls it seeing the risen Lord; Luke describes a Christophany-without-visual-Christ followed by blindness. The deeper contradiction is whether Paul's experience was the same kind of event as the Twelve's encounters with the risen Jesus — a question with major implications for the historicity of the resurrection appearances. Bart Ehrman and Dale Allison both treat Paul's experience as visionary, which would also reframe what the earlier appearances were.

entries.question: Who forces non-believers to disbelieve?
entries.summary: John 12:40 attributes the blinding of unbelievers' eyes to God, and 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12 has God sending strong delusion so that they will believe a lie and be damned. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 instead attributes the blinding of unbelievers' minds to the god of this world (Satan). The New Testament cannot agree on whether divine or demonic agency is responsible for unbelief.
entries.commentary: The Johannine reading (John 12:40) quotes Isaiah 6:10 and applies the prophet's hardening commission to Jesus' Jewish opponents — God himself is the grammatical subject doing the blinding. 2 Thessalonians 2:11 extends this with God actively sending a *plane* (delusion) so that unbelievers will believe the lie and be judged. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 attributes the same outcome — blinded minds among the perishing — to *ho theos tou aiōnos toutou*, the god of this age, almost universally understood as Satan. The standard apologetic harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and Thomas Schreiner, distinguishes ultimate from proximate causation: God ordains the blinding, Satan executes it, and human beings choose unbelief, so all three layers can be true simultaneously. That layered Calvinistic compatibilism does dissolve the formal contradiction — but only by importing a theological framework not present in the texts themselves. Critical scholarship from Raymond Brown on John, Victor Furnish on 2 Corinthians, and Abraham Malherbe on Thessalonians treats these passages as reflecting different theodicies developed independently in different early Christian communities. The Johannine community needed to explain why fellow Jews rejected Jesus and read Isaiah's hardening motif onto them. The Pauline Corinthian context needed to explain why his own gospel was rejected and reached for the Satan-as-blinder image. 2 Thessalonians, generally regarded as deutero-Pauline, develops an eschatological account where God's judgment includes hardening. These are three different etiologies of unbelief stitched into a single canon. The compatibilist harmonization rescues coherence but it isn't what any of the texts is doing on its own terms.

entries.question: Did Paul visit all of the disciples when he went to Jerusalem after his conversion?
entries.summary: Acts 9:26-28 has Paul, after his conversion, mingling freely with the disciples in Jerusalem, going in and out among them. Paul's own first-person account in Galatians 1:18-19 says he went to Jerusalem only after three years, stayed fifteen days with Peter, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother. Acts and Paul disagree on both the timeline and the breadth of the meeting.
entries.commentary: This is one of the foundational tensions in critical New Testament scholarship — the disagreement between Acts and Paul's autobiographical statements in Galatians 1-2. Galatians 1 is Paul under oath, defending his apostolic independence by emphasizing how little contact he had with the Jerusalem leadership: *eis Hierosolyma historēsai Kēphan*, to inquire of Cephas, fifteen days, no other apostles except James. Acts 9:26-28 describes the same trip but has Paul joining the disciples broadly, with Barnabas vouching for him to the apostles plural, and Paul moving freely *eis to onoma tou kyriou*. The standard apologetic harmonization, found in F. F. Bruce and Darrell Bock, says Acts gives a general summary while Galatians gives specifics, so when Acts says "the apostles" it really means Peter and James, the only two Paul mentions. That works grammatically — Acts is often loose with collective terms — but it strains plausibility when you stack the divergences. Paul also says the Judean churches did not know him by sight (Gal 1:22), which directly contradicts Luke's picture of Paul moving in and out openly in Jerusalem. Critical scholars including John Knox, Robert Jewett, and Gerd Lüdemann have argued that Luke is constructing a harmonized narrative of early Christian unity that doesn't match Paul's own polemical defense in Galatians. Luke's program is to show continuity and integration between Paul and the Jerusalem apostles; Paul's program in Galatians is to show his independence from them. The contradictions in details flow directly from the different theological projects. Paul, as his own primary source, has priority over Luke writing decades later.

entries.question: Should we bear each other's burdens?
entries.summary: Galatians 6:2 commands believers to bear one another's burdens. Three verses later, Galatians 6:5 says every person shall bear his own burden. The same paragraph from the same author gives diametrically opposite directives about whose burden you carry.
entries.commentary: This one rewards lexical attention because Paul uses two different Greek words. In 6:2 the word is *barē* (heavy weights, burdens, troubles); in 6:5 the word is *phortion* (a load, a soldier's pack, sometimes one's own assigned task). The distinction is real and well-documented in BDAG. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker, and Ben Witherington, leverages this distinction: *barē* refers to the crushing weights of life that the community helps shoulder, while *phortion* refers to one's own God-given assignment or moral accountability that no one else can carry for you. Read this way, the paragraph is internally coherent — share crises, but own your own responsibilities — and 6:5 may even allude to eschatological judgment ("each will give an account of himself before God," Rom 14:12). Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz and J. Louis Martyn largely agrees this is the correct reading; the verb in 6:5 is future tense (*bastasei*) and points toward the day of judgment, when each person stands alone for their own works. So the apparent contradiction here is largely an artifact of the KJV's translation of both *barē* and *phortion* as "burden." In modern translations the tension visibly softens. This entry should probably be flagged as overstated — the contradiction is more lexical artifact than substantive theological conflict. There remains a genuine pastoral tension between communal solidarity and individual moral accountability, but Paul is making both points deliberately, not contradicting himself.

entries.question: Should believers discuss their faith with non-believers?
entries.summary: 1 Peter 3:15 commands believers to be ready always to give an answer to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope in them. Colossians 4:5-6 echoes this with speech seasoned with salt toward outsiders. But 2 John 1:10 forbids even receiving anyone who brings a different doctrine into your house, and 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16 command shunning profane and vain babblings. Engage outsiders, or shun them — the New Testament does both.
entries.commentary: The texts are talking past each other because they assume different audiences. 1 Peter 3:15 envisions a Christian minority pressed by hostile outsiders demanding to know why these people are different — the *apologia* (defense) is reactive and requires intelligible engagement. Colossians 4:5-6 likewise prescribes outward-facing speech. The Johannine and Pastoral texts envision a different scenario: itinerant teachers carrying heterodox versions of the gospel into believing households, where the rule becomes shun-and-don't-engage. 2 John 1:10's prohibition is specifically about the docetist Christology that the Johannine letters fight throughout (1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7). The Pastorals' "profane babblings" (*bebēlous kenophōnias*) refers to proto-Gnostic speculation. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by Karen Jobes and George Knight, says these texts address different scenarios: outsiders genuinely seeking get an apologia; insider teachers spreading false doctrine get shunned. That distinction is real and largely correct as exegesis. The contradiction is partially overstated by SAB's framing, but it isn't fully resolved either. The Pastoral epistles deploy *kenophōnias* and the Johannine letters deploy heretic-shunning language in ways that have historically been weaponized against any external engagement, and the texts themselves don't sharply mark the in-group/out-group distinction the harmonization requires. The contradiction is functionally less about whether to discuss faith with non-believers and more about how internally consistent the NT is on doctrinal engagement with dissenters. A coherency note is warranted.

entries.question: Is the day of the Lord at hand?
entries.summary: 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 has Paul including himself among "we who are alive and remain" until the Lord's coming — assuming an imminent parousia within his own lifetime. 2 Thessalonians 2:2-3 explicitly tells the same community not to think the day of Christ is at hand, because there must first be the apostasy and the revealing of the man of sin. The two letters give incompatible timelines for the eschaton.
entries.commentary: This contradiction is one of the central reasons critical scholarship overwhelmingly regards 2 Thessalonians as pseudonymous — written in Paul's name by a later author trying to dampen apocalyptic enthusiasm that 1 Thessalonians had stoked. 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 places Paul squarely in the "we who are alive and remain" cohort; he expects to be raptured up to meet the Lord in the air without dying first. By the time you reach 2 Thessalonians 2:2-3, the message has flipped: the day hasn't come, an apostasy must occur first, the man of sin must be revealed, and the present restrainer must be removed. This is precisely the kind of delay-theology you find in late first-century texts that are trying to manage the failure of the imminent parousia (compare 2 Peter 3:8-9). Apologetic harmonizers like F. F. Bruce and Gene Green argue that even in 1 Thessalonians Paul never specifies a date and the "we" is rhetorical, while 2 Thessalonians clarifies the order of events without rejecting imminence. That reading is grammatically possible but minimizes Paul's natural identification with "we who are alive." Critical scholarship from Wolfgang Trilling, Maarten Menken, and Margaret MacDonald has built a strong case that 2 Thessalonians is a deliberate corrective written by a Paulinist after Paul's death, when the parousia hadn't materialized and Paul's authentic letters were generating problematic eschatological excitement. The verbal echoes of 1 Thessalonians in 2 Thessalonians — combined with the theological reversal — fit a forgery designed to defuse the original letter. The contradiction is real, and it has the additional consequence that 2 Thessalonians is best read as evidence of post-apostolic disappointment.

entries.question: Can the devil capture us at will?
entries.summary: 2 Timothy 2:26 describes the devil holding people captive at his will. James 4:7 says if you resist the devil, he will flee from you. One text portrays the devil as able to take people captive at his own discretion; the other portrays him as easily repelled by ordinary resistance.
entries.commentary: The contradiction here is partly translation-driven. The Greek of 2 Timothy 2:26 is *ezōgrēmenoi hyp' autou eis to ekeinou thelēma*, which has been read two ways. The KJV-style reading takes both pronouns as referring to the devil: "taken captive by him at his will." An alternative reading, defended by I. Howard Marshall and others, takes the first pronoun as referring to the devil but the second as referring to God: taken captive by the devil to do God's will (since the people are recovering themselves from the devil's snare). On the latter reading the verse no longer claims the devil captures people at his unilateral discretion. James 4:7 is straightforward: resist the devil and he will flee. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by Peter Davids and Douglas Moo, takes the Pastoral verse to mean that those *outside* the believing community are subject to the devil's will, while James addresses those who *are* in the community and can resist effectively. The harmonization holds if you accept the pronoun ambiguity in 2 Timothy and the in-out distinction in application. Critical scholarship from Raymond Collins and Luke Timothy Johnson generally accepts that 2 Timothy is conceptually closer to a deterministic captivity model than James' resistance model, reflecting different anthropologies in different streams of early Christianity. The Pastorals lean toward a more pessimistic view of unaided human ability against demonic power; James is closer to early Jewish wisdom traditions where moral resistance is straightforward. The contradiction is real but soft, and partially mitigated by the pronoun ambiguity in the Greek. A coherency note about the lexical/pronoun issue is warranted.

entries.question: Did Enoch die?
entries.summary: Hebrews 11:13 lists Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and Sarah and says "these all died." Eight verses earlier the same chapter, Hebrews 11:5, explicitly says Enoch was translated so that he should not see death — echoing Genesis 5:24 where God simply took him. The same author appears to both deny and affirm Enoch's death within one chapter.
entries.commentary: This is the rare contradiction where the author actually does seem to trip over himself, but careful reading mitigates the problem. Hebrews 11:5 is unambiguous about Enoch: he was translated (*metetethē*) so that he should not see death. Hebrews 11:13 then says *kata pistin apethanon houtoi pantes* — "according to faith these all died" — within a paragraph that lists Abraham and Sarah, but the immediate antecedent of "these all" is contested. Apologetic harmonization, defended by William Lane and Harold Attridge, takes 11:13 to refer specifically to the patriarchal figures mentioned in 11:8-12 (Abraham, Sarah, and their descendants), not to Abel and Enoch from earlier in the chapter. On this reading, "these all" is restrictive to the immediately preceding cluster, and Enoch is excluded by 11:5. The Greek grammar is genuinely ambiguous, and the immediate-antecedent reading is plausible. Critical scholarship from Attridge, Craig Koester, and Luke Timothy Johnson largely accepts this restrictive reading; the author of Hebrews knew his own claim about Enoch in 11:5 and is unlikely to have contradicted it eight verses later. The contradiction is more apparent than real and depends on reading "these all" maximally. There is still some literary tension because the chapter's opening cluster of figures includes Abel and Enoch, and the average reader hits 11:13 and naturally folds them back in. A coherency note is warranted: the contradiction is grammatically resolvable and probably overstated by the SAB framing.

entries.question: Was Rahab saved by faith or works?
entries.summary: Hebrews 11:31 says Rahab the harlot did not perish with the disobedient because of her faith when she received the spies. James 2:25 says Rahab was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way. Same Old Testament figure, same single act (hiding the Israelite spies in Joshua 2), two contradictory verdicts on what saved her.
entries.commentary: This is the same Pauline-vs-Jacobean tension that appears around Abraham (see id 542), now applied to Rahab. Hebrews places Rahab in its great roll-call of faith heroes — *pistei Raab hē pornē* — and credits her preservation to faith. James 2:25 zeroes in on the same episode and credits her justification to works (*ex ergōn*). Both texts cite the same act: hospitable concealment of the spies. The harmonization, articulated by Douglas Moo and Peter Davids, runs through the faith-as-demonstrated-by-works framework: Rahab's reception of the spies was the visible expression of her underlying faith, so both authors are describing the same reality from different angles. That harmonization works at the systematic-theology level but it requires importing later categories — the medieval *fides quae* / *fides qua* distinction, or Reformation faith-and-works syntheses — that neither author articulates. Critical scholarship from Luke Timothy Johnson, Dale Allison, and Harold Attridge treats Hebrews 11 as drawing on Jewish-Hellenistic exemplar traditions (Sirach 44, 4 Maccabees) where faith and faithful action are intertwined, while James 2 is explicitly polemicizing against a faith-alone reading — likely a misreading of Paul. The contradiction reflects two early Christian streams disagreeing about how Rahab's salvation works, with both texts authorized as canonical scripture. Whatever harmonization is possible at the doctrinal level, the canonical text places these two verdicts in unresolved juxtaposition. Rahab is the rare figure both authors reach for, and that's exactly why the disagreement is sharpest.
